title: Viola
summary: A computed viola, outside the real spread: mostly too dark, attacks far too quick, a noisy band near 395 Hz that is ours. E3 and Gb5 sound 12.1 and 11.6 cents sharp (finger at the equal-tempered station); C4 and Db4 have it moved to the note. Every note is a string with diameters read from photographs of a playing viola, bowed by a finite-width bow with hair compliance on the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025), driving a computed shell body (Cassavetti Stradivari outline, 209 modes) and its air cavity at 144 kHz. On D4, A4, C4 and Db4 the bow force follows bow speed at the start of the stroke; G3 and C3 have their after-length moved off the exact sixth by the cello's printed ratio, borrowed. G3, C3, D4 and Db4 carry the shell's wood loss raised 3.25 times, because the body's mode near 395 Hz reads Q 75 against 15 to 27 printed; A4, E3, Gb5 and C4 each lost grader rows with it and keep their earlier render.
physics_present: a computed viola shell body: the outline of the Cassavetti Stradivari viola (Library of Congress), f-holes from its caliper sheet, plate thicknesses from Johannsson's viola table, spruce top and maple back and ribs, a 6.5 mm mesh and all 209 modes its 15 Hz to 5 kHz window holds; the string drives it through bridge flexibility; a 3.24 L air cavity through a physical neck; dry room air; played at 144 kHz on every note
the friction law measured on real rosin (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13), on every page

strings with diameters measured on a playing viola (Percival 2013, Table 3.2, from photographs, about 10 %), tension and density from Guettler; the bending stiffness is derived from Percival's measured inharmonicity, because no source prints a viola string's stiffness
a bow of finite width with hair compliance, and bridge and bow flexibility
the after-length (bridge to tailpiece) at one sixth of the speaking length; on G3 and C3 it is the sixth times 116/115, the cello's printed ratio, borrowed because no source prints a viola's

stopped notes (E3, C4, Db4, Gb5): a rigid finger on the fingerboard (Issanchou 2017), a 1e13 N/m stop and a 3.5 N press; at its equal-tempered station on E3 and Gb5, and on C4 and Db4 moved to the note by one correction of 14.5 cents, the sharpness measured on the same string's phrase renders, with the bow at 1/11 of the sounding length from the bridge
on D4, A4, C4 and Db4 the bow force follows bow speed through the start of the stroke (Schelleng: both force limits scale with bow speed); the ramp, the final force and the release are unchanged

G3, C3, D4 and Db4: the shell body's wood loss raised 3.25 times (FoggyHill's loss packs on the spruce top and the maple back and ribs), because the body's bridge-coupled mode near 395 Hz reads Q 75 on this body against 15 to 27 printed for a viola (Coffey 2016, self-published); on C3 it is what lets the grader read the shell render as the named note, and on Db4 it also lowers the third harmonic, which sits on the shell's second bridge-coupled mode near 834 Hz. A4, E3, Gb5 and C4 were rendered with it too: the line near 395 Hz fell on each, but each lost one to three grader rows, so those pages keep their earlier render
physics_missing: the shell's modal mass at the bridge is light against print: the body's bridge-coupled mode near 395 Hz has an effective mass of 34 g, where a printed viola's peaks give 56 to 117 g (Maestre, Scavone and Smith 2013, Fig. 4, one McGill viola, Q read from the figure), and the engine has no card knob for it; raising the wood loss 3.25 times lowers that peak 9 dB and leaves it 12 to 15 dB over the print

the finger moved to the note on E3 and Gb5: they sound sharp of equal temperament (E3 +12.1 c, Gb5 +11.6 c on the posted pages), where the recordings sit below it; on C4 and Db4 the one correction puts the grader's pitch at -1.8 c and +4.8 c, against recordings at -1.4 c and -22.1 c

what drives a noisy band of lines around the shell's 400.8 Hz pole (strongest near 395 Hz, noise-driven and not a comb, the same place when the note changes) and a fixed line near 200 Hz on the viola pages: neither is explained

the tone and the start of the note: most notes are too dark (D4 centroid 568 Hz against 1210 Hz in the recording) and start far faster than the recordings (D4 attack 104 to 292 ms against 604 ms; C4 107 ms against 342 ms)
harmonics-to-noise as high as the recordings: ours is lower on the pages that state it (C4 16.0 dB against 30.0 dB, Db4 23.5 dB against 33.0 dB)
string loss and bending stiffness from a source: no loss is printed for these strings, so the cards carry none, and the stiffness is derived

the viola pages that carry the wood loss raised 3.25 times (G3, C3, D4 and Db4) apply it at every frequency, a factor set on the body's lowest strong pole (Q 75 on the wood alone against 15 to 27 printed); on D4's loaded response it takes the body's pressure per newton down by 4.5, 5.9 and 5.8 dB (medians over 1.0 to 1.6, 1.6 to 2.4 and 2.4 to 3.5 kHz) and sharp peaks by more, one at 2.36 kHz by 14 dB, and the posted page's lines sit within 1.7 dB of that loaded response; that is about half of the 13 dB by which the viola D4 page's lines at the 6th to 11th harmonic sit below the violin D4 page's, which carries wood alone; the rest is 2 to 3 dB of bridge force (the viola string's after-length makes holes at the 6th and 12th harmonics, 12 dB each) and about 4 dB that nothing here accounts for; whether the loss should rise with frequency is not known
